answer:
The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7. QB12 is the middle qubit.

How I picked it. I read garnet's current default calibration set (f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). It has 28 calibrated CZ pairs, and every pair has an interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) fidelity. I checked every chain of 3 qubits that is joined by two calibrated CZ pairs, and I multiplied the two fidelities for each chain.
- The CZ on QB11-QB12 has fidelity 0.998693.
- The CZ on QB12-QB7 has fidelity 0.998016.
- Their product is 0.996712. That is the highest of all chains.
- Second place is QB12-QB11-QB16 with 0.994689. Third place is QB18-QB19-QB20 with 0.993989.

What I ran. I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB11, QB12 and QB7.
1. A half-turn rotation puts each of the 3 qubits into an equal mix of 0 and 1.
2. A CZ runs on QB11-QB12, then a CZ runs on QB12-QB7. These are the only two-qubit gates.
3. Rotations on QB11 and QB7 turn the result into the GHZ state.
4. All 3 qubits are measured.

A noise-free simulation of this exact gate list gives 000 half the time and 111 half the time. I read the circuit back from the server. It holds 2 CZ gates on those two pairs, it measures QB11, QB12 and QB7, and it uses 200 shots. Job ID: 01a160a5-6866-759e-ac3e-70c393471e43, run on garnet:mock.

The counts are in the order QB11 QB12 QB7: 000: 52, 111: 55, 100: 51, 011: 42. The mock machine does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bitstrings, so these counts do not show GHZ behavior. The outcomes 100 and 011 would be rare on a perfect device.

The principle. In a GHZ state, the 3 qubits are linked so that they all read 0 or all read 1. Each reading is a coin flip, but the 3 qubits always agree. Every CZ gate adds some error, so the chain whose two gates have the highest product of fidelities should give the cleanest GHZ state on the real QPU. A run on real garnet would test that, but it costs credits, so I did not run it.
